column3: States the same worship test in terms of an object's lack of ownership over harm and benefit.
Introduces the nearby Abraham sequence but adds no direct account of the idols' incapacity.
Directly condemns calling on another than God that can neither harm nor benefit.
Abraham's appeal to his father adds the idols' failure to hear, see, or avail anything.
Opens the local inquiry into the images to which Abraham's people remain devoted.
Presents the harm-benefit question itself as the decisive test of the worshiped objects.
Repeats the powerless-object test while adding that its worshiper supplies misplaced support.
The immediate sequel denounces worship of beings besides God as an abandonment of reason.
Tests proposed gods against their inability to avert harm or provide rescue through intercession.
Challenges the choice of intercessors who possess neither anything nor understanding.
Directly prohibits calling on another than God that can neither benefit nor harm.
Benefit from remembrance of believers does not clarify the worship-power test.
Denies that the worshiped beings possess provision or any capacity to supply it.
Continues the surrounding passage but adds no focused element to the idol critique.
Created benefits and drinks are unrelated to the claimed agency of worshiped objects.
Adds the intercessory claim made for beings that neither harm nor benefit.
Advances Abraham's intention to act against the idols, preparing their public test.
Limits harm to God's permission, but concerns satanic whispering rather than worshiped objects.
The futility of fleeing death or killing is not an idol-agency test.
The challenge to ask the chief idol if it can speak directly exposes their lack of agency.
Addresses the limited injury opponents can cause, not false worship.
The ineffectiveness of counsel under divine willing is outside the idol critique.
Reopens Abraham's question to his people about what they worship.
Benefit from admonition is unrelated to the focus's causal test.
The lack of benefit in shared punishment does not concern worshiped intermediaries.
Provides the immediate scriptural setting, without developing the images' powerlessness.
Its broad contrast of what benefits people with vanishing falsehood is only a distant analogy.
Concerns protection from opponents' plotting, not worship or independent agency.
Shows the idolaters answering the challenge by trying to defend their gods through fire.
Uses the same mutual harm-benefit incapacity formula in an eschatological setting.
Abraham refuses fear of associates except under his Lord's will, locating effective power with God.
The idolaters concede that the images cannot speak, immediately grounding the focus's question.
The failure of intercession to benefit on the final day only indirectly parallels false reliance.
Jacob's complaint to God does not address the agency of worshiped beings.
Names the people's settled devotion to idols in the parallel Abraham narrative.
The messenger's denial of power over harm or guidance qualifies creaturely agency, though not idol worship.
Personal guidance and misguidance do not develop the focus's worship test.
Establishes Abraham's discernment at the opening of the local idol episode.
The balance of benefit and sin in wine and gambling is unrelated to worshiped beings.
Musa's request for pardon does not illuminate harm-benefit agency.
God's command changing the fire's effect demonstrates that physical power is not independent.
The messenger denies independent benefit and harm even for himself, explicitly subject to God's will.
Rejects the attribution of divinity to created persons besides God.
The question whether idols hear their callers supplies a further agency test.
Magic's harm and lack of benefit are restricted by God's permission, but the subject is not idol worship.
Denies creative power to those invoked besides God, broadening the case for their incapacity.
Records the people's appeal to inherited devotion to the images.
Returns both blessings and distress-response to God, without examining a false object of worship.
God's ability to bring an announced matter concerns neither idols nor the benefit-harm test.
The failure of the plot against Abraham continues the narrative reversal of the idolaters' effort.
Humans cannot harm God by refusing to mobilize; this does not clarify idol worship.
Divine justice toward servants offers no focused relation to the candidate theme.
The calf's failure to answer and to own harm or benefit closely parallels the focus's test.
Faith benefiting a community is a different use of benefit from an object's claimed power.
The reassurance of Abraham about good news is unrelated to the idol episode's test.
Abraham's verdict of manifest error on his people and their fathers interprets their idol devotion.
Shows a supposed patron whose harm is nearer than benefit, a contrasting false-reliance formulation.
Denies false gods ownership of harm, benefit, death, life, and resurrection.
The breaking of the images stages the concrete challenge to their claimed power.
The final-day inability of wealth and children to benefit is not about worshiped agents.
Rejects reciprocal worship but adds no account of why the worshiped objects lack power.
The people's question about Abraham's seriousness continues the immediate dispute.
Permitted benefits from sacrificial animals are unrelated to the focus's false-object critique.
Directly rejects calling on another than God that cannot benefit or harm, adding the consequence of reversal.
Treating desire as a god broadens misplaced worship but does not apply the harm-benefit test.
The uselessness of excuses on the final day is unrelated to claimed divine agency.
Contrasts refusing worship of others besides God with worship of the God who takes life.
Abraham identifies the true Lord as the Creator, countering the people's devotion to images.
Physical impairment in the comparison of believers is unrelated to harm as causal power.
Mentions worshiped beings without specifying their inability or a worship critique.
The people's alarm over their gods after their destruction advances the local exposure.
The uselessness of excuses for wrongdoers does not clarify the focus's agency question.
The reciprocal non-worship declaration remains too general after the direct idol tests.
Revelation's source does not illuminate idols' ability to benefit or harm.
The messenger denies self-owned harm and benefit except as God wills, qualifying all creaturely agency.
False protectors fail to avail against punishment, but the relation is less direct than the leading tests.
The calf presented as a god supplies the object later tested for speech and harm-benefit ownership.
Divine removal of distress and human persistence does not concern worshiped objects.
God alone removes the impending event, an indirect affirmation of exclusive effective power.
Speech not from desire does not add to the worship-power question.
The conditional benefit of reminder is unrelated to independent agency.
Rejects associating partners or taking human lords besides God, though without the specific utility test.
The lack of permission to offer excuses is unrelated to false worship.
Benefits from livestock do not clarify an idol's claimed causal power.
Those called besides God possess nothing in the heavens or earth and provide no support.
The communication of revelation to God's servant is outside the idol critique.
A person's claim over mercy after distress only distantly concerns mistaken attribution of benefit.
Prohibits worship of those called besides God and contrasts it with guided refusal.
The buyer's hoped-for benefit from Joseph has no relation to worshiped agency.
The invoked beings cannot create even a fly or recover what it takes, vividly demonstrating powerlessness.
The divine warning against returning to a wrongdoing is unrelated to the focus.
Forbids obeying pressure to associate partners with God, but offers no specific agency test.
The regret of disbelievers and concealment of speech do not bear on idol power.
Instructions on prayer, recitation, and charity do not clarify the focus's causal claim.
The resurrection sign concerns God's power but does not add to the false-worship test.
God's will over trial and purification only indirectly underscores that no one can control outcomes against Him.
Household etiquette and prohibition of harm to the Prophet are unrelated to the focus.
The command to fear God and obey the messenger adds no focused account of false worship.
The inheritance and ranks of servants do not develop the harm-benefit critique.
The cosmic warning signs do not address worshiped beings or their claimed utility.
Denies that the worshiped names have any God-given authority and reserves judgment and worship for God.
In severe distress, calling is directed to God rather than the alleged associates.
States that God alone is called in distress and may remove the harm for which others are associated.
Challenges associating beings that create nothing and are themselves created.
Denies that the associates can help either their worshipers or themselves.
Exposes the inability of the invoked beings to answer or follow a call.
Describes those called besides God as servants unable to answer their callers.
Tests the alleged partners for bodily faculties and effective action, including hearing and sight.
The alleged partners disavow the worship directed to them on the final day.
God's sufficient witness over the worship relation adds only an indirect clarification.
Contrasts God's true call with other calls that cannot answer their supplicants.
Describes the beings invoked besides God as dead rather than living and unaware of resurrection.
Denies that those called besides God can remove or transfer affliction.
Shows sought intermediaries themselves seeking nearness, mercy, and protection from God.
In distress at sea, all those called besides God disappear from reliance.
Challenges the adoption of gods besides God without clear authority.
Identifies the taking of gods besides God in the expectation of honor or strength.
Foresees those gods rejecting their worshipers and becoming adversaries to them.
Aaron explicitly warns that the calf is only a trial and directs worship to the Merciful.
Records the people's persistence in devotion to the calf despite that warning.
Challenges the taking of gods besides God and demands proof for the association.
Questions whether alleged gods can protect their worshipers from God.
Condemns worship of that for which God has sent no authority or proof.
Treats calling another god alongside God as a claim without proof and denies success to its maker.
On the final day, the worshiped beings deny that they led their worshipers astray.
The idolaters acknowledge inherited worship in answer to Abraham's inquiry.
Abraham directs attention to the objects his people and their forebears worship.
Includes the inherited objects of worship within Abraham's challenge.
Abraham disavows the worshiped objects as enemies except the Lord of the worlds.
The associates cannot answer when God calls for those whom people claimed as partners.
The partners are summoned but cannot respond, exposing the false call.
Repeats the final summons for claimed partners, reinforcing their absence and inability.
Denies provision to what is worshiped besides God and redirects the search for provision to God.
Denies that the associators will have intercessors among their alleged partners.
Uses a human ownership analogy to reject treating servants as partners with equal authority.
Challenges the alleged partners to show what they have created.
Limits intercession to those granted permission, constraining claims made for intermediaries.
Those called besides God do not possess even the smallest share of dominion.
Those invoked besides God neither hear the call nor could answer it, and will deny the association.
Challenges alleged partners to show what they created or possess as a share in creation.
Identifies the taking of gods besides God in the hope of receiving help.
Denies that the gods can help their worshipers, despite the worshipers' attendance upon them.
Abraham questions the idols directly about their failure to speak.
Challenges worship of objects that people themselves carve.
Attributes the creation of both worshipers and what they make to God.
Reports the claim that protectors besides God are worshiped only to bring people near to Him.
Tests the alleged beings against their inability to remove harm or withhold mercy when God wills it.
Assigns all intercession to God, countering independent intercessory claims.
Contrasts God's judgment with the incapacity of those called besides Him to judge anything.
Abraham declares himself free of what his people worship.
Excepts the Creator from Abraham's disavowal and identifies Him as the proper guide.
Challenges alleged partners to show what they created or their share in the heavens and earth.
Calls those invoked besides God most astray because they cannot answer until the Day of Resurrection.
The worshiped beings will become enemies of their worshipers and reject their worship.
Introduces the named goddesses as objects of the association under critique.
Reduces the alleged gods to names without God-given authority, governed instead by conjecture and desire.
Forbids calling anyone alongside God in places of worship.
